highlights.title: Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down
highlights.summary: The call comes amid growing concerns that AI models may become able to inflict serious damage worldwide.
body: The head of AI company Anthropic has called for the pace of development of artificial intelligence models to slow down and to be closely monitored.
In an essay, Dario Amodei said developing AI was not in question, but the risks associated with it were "serious" and companies and governments must be given time to address them.
The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei.

There have been growing concerns recently about the technology's potential risks. An AI researcher who left Anthropic this week told the BBC that "if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future".

highlights.title: Perplexity trusts GPT-6 Astra with end-to-end systems
highlights.summary: Perplexity uses Astra to write communications, change software, and monitor production systems, and checks in much less frequently than with earlier models.
body: As an AI-powered answer engine, Perplexity is deeply focused on search and accuracy. Its ability to process large amounts of information is critically important. Johnny Ho, Cofounder and Chief Strategy Officer, observes that every time the model gets better at writing code, Perplexity’s search engine improves too. It becomes able to write better programs that search the web and internal information and summarize it very concisely.
But the real challenge, according to Johnny, is taking those informational aspects and applying them to real-world systems. Something made easier with GPT‑6 Astra.
For Johnny, one of the most useful applications of AI is testing code. With limited time to test manually, he asks GPT‑6 Astra to build a small testing program around an application.

The model generates realistic responses like those another service would send, for example, a language model API or a connector. By standing in for those services, the model can check how the application responds and test the workflow from start to finish.

body: Shelton is the first black American man to reach the US Open final since Arthur Ashe in 1972, and is aiming to become the first home male player to win the title since Andy Roddick in 2003.
He will have a raucous Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd behind him when he takes on German top seed and title favourite Zverev.
Shelton revealed he took advice from Rafael Nadal before his break-out run in New York.
The 23-year-old from Florida beat compatriot Frances Tiafoe to set up a winner-takes-all showdown with Zverev, who dispatched Karen Khachanov.

highlights.title: Overwatch's New Hero Doctrine: Full Ability Kit and Perks Revealed at BlizzCon
highlights.summary: Overwatch 's new hero Doctrine was revealed Saturday at BlizzCon 2026 and pitched by Blizzard Entertainment as a vampire-inspired support hero with a high mechanical floor.
body: At BlizzCon, we got our first hands-on experience with Doctrine, and a look at the full kit of Doomfist's old ally. While Doctrine does have some complexity to his suite of abilities, he's instantly fun to play with, with elements that will appeal to offense-minded healers, Reaper players who get queued into support, and anyone with a bit of a goth streak.

Doctrine's weapon, Eternal Scepter, functions much like the primary weapons of Juno, Ana, and Jetpack Cat, in that it both heals allies and damages enemies with unified fire. That helps to simplify his kit somewhat, as players will be able to Infuse it to give his shots more oomph. Shrouded Momentum is basically Doctrine's version of Reaper's Wraith Form, while Invigorating Drones gives him an alternate healing option.

Doctrine's Perks offer some surprisingly conflicting choices, letting players choose which type of healing to boost at level 2, and a rare overall hit point reduction in favor of stronger Eternal Scepter healing output. With what feels like a long cooldown timer on Infuse, it will be a tough decision on which level 3 perk to go after in the heat of battle.

highlights.title: I survived a stroke during an ocean swim. Here’s what I’ve learned about fear
highlights.summary: After his stroke in rough surf, Graham Russell embarked on an unexpected journey into fear. Three lessons helped him return to the joy of the ocean. Looking out over the ocean, I would watch the waves sparkling in the sunlight as they grew and spilled into a burst of froth.
body: In winter last year I tore the lining of an artery in my neck during a rough ocean swim off the Central Coast of New South Wales. It caused a stroke while I was in the water, which saw me scrambling back to shore where a surfer noticed me and sounded the alarm. Six months later, the injury had healed, and my motor functions were all back to normal. But as I prepared for a dip in calm conditions on a sunny day in January, I paused. An unexpected journey into fear began.
Standing on the sand, a thousand scenarios would play out in my mind: how big was that wave? Was it powerful enough to injure me? Where would the currents take me? Would I be safe?

I assumed I already knew what fear felt like – I had surfed in rough conditions before, saved lives in the ocean and pursued plenty of adventure in my early years – but this was different. This was fear in the total absence of any bravado or exhilaration or reward. It did not feel like a physical challenge to surmount, it felt simply like my energy would disappear and I would sink beneath the waves.
points: After his stroke in rough surf, Graham Russell embarked on an unexpected journey into fear.
Three lessons helped him return to the joy of the ocean.
Looking out over the ocean, I would watch the waves sparkling in the sunlight as they grew and spilled into a burst of froth.

highlights.title: Trump is giving data centers a pass to pollute
highlights.summary: President Donald Trump is weakening environmental regulations in the name of speeding up the construction of AI data centers, raising health risks for Americans, a cadre of former EPA officials said this week in a briefing and new report.
body: The Trump administration is sacrificing Americans’ health to build data centers, former EPA officials warn.

At the start of his term, Trump’s EPA administrator, Lee Zeldin, proclaimed his goal of making America “ the AI capital of the world ” through deregulation. Since then, Zeldin and the White House have rolled back dozens of rules on top of cutting staff and funding at the US EPA.

As a result of the Trump administration’s deregulation spree and attacks on renewable energy, the wave of new AI data centers is increasingly powered by dirty energy that can impact Americans’ health even if they don’t live near a data center, the group of EPA alumni warn. They say that the agency they once worked for, which was created to “ protect human health and the environment,” is no longer the watchdog it should be as the physical infrastructure underpinning generative AI changes America’s landscape.
“You would think that an industry buildout of this magnitude, billed as a revolution, would mean more vigilance from EPA.”

highlights.title: Guimaraes haunts Sunderland as Arsenal continue winning start
highlights.summary: Bruno Guimaraes scored a stunning goal two minutes after David Raya had saved a penalty as Arsenal beat Sunderland 2-0 to move above Manchester City at the top of the Premier League.
body: The Black Cats had the chance to go in front when Ezri Konsa was penalised for holding Dan Ballard in the second half but Raya brilliantly tipped Enzo Le Fee's spot kick onto the post.

Just 121 seconds later, Guimaraes, whose every touch had been booed by the home fans due to his Newcastle connections, crashed a stunning strike in off the underside of the crossbar from outside the Sunderland box for his first Arsenal goal.

Arsenal had to withstand late pressure from the home side, with Raya saving well from Nordi Mukiele, but they made the result safe when Bukayo Saka scored a stoppage-time penalty after Reinildo Mandava was shown a second yellow card for hauling him down.

The victory, Arsenal's fourth in a row in the Premier League and sixth in all competitions, maintains their strong start to the campaign and puts the champions three points above Manchester City, who face Manchester United live on Sky Sports on Sunday.

highlights.title: OpenAI’s Sam Altman says it would be ‘ill-advised’ to go public in 2026
highlights.summary: While OpenAI has filed confidentially for an IPO, the company will not be going public this year, according to CEO Sam Altman.
body: Altman was interviewed recently by Fortune editor in chief Alyson Shontell; amidst the fallout from the OpenAI-HuggingFace hack, as well as broader discussions about AI safety, Shontell asked whether OpenAI still feels pressure to “move really fast” due to its IPO plans.
“We’re not rushing into an IPO,” Altman said. “I actually think that given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public.”

Instead, he insisted that OpenAI will go public “when we’re ready, which is when the business is ready, when we feel ready from what the moment is like in society with this technology.” When pressed on whether that means the IPO isn’t happening in 2026, Altman replied, “I would say not 2026, yeah. We’ve got a lot of stuff to do.”

The New York Times reported in June that although OpenAI had hired bankers and lawyers with the goal of going public in the third or fourth quarter of 2026, the company was leaning toward 2027 due to the volatility of tech stocks and its own financial challenges.

highlights.title: Brits Skupski, Hewett clinch respective US Open doubles, wheelchair titles
highlights.summary: There was double success for Britain at the US Open on Saturday, with Alfie Hewett regaining his wheelchair singles title and Neal Skupski finally claiming the men’s doubles crown.
body: Emotional Hewett burst into tears after beating Tokito Oda 6-0 7-6 (7-5) to deny the 20-year-old Japanese star a calendar Grand Slam.
The 28-year-old, who was beaten by Oda in the finals of the French Open and Wimbledon this year, said: "It's taken lot of hard work, a lot of soul-searching at times, a lot of reflecting.

"The Wimbledon pumping was a tough one to swallow. I definitely came away from that one with a lot of regret, took some time off and had a hard, long look in the mirror about who I wanted to be on the tennis court and how I wanted to show up.

"Today I didn't care about the outcome. It was about being a little bit more like 'Alfie' and showing the fight and showing the grit and the desire to go out and play a bit more fearless. I think the performance showed that."

highlights.title: X-Men Star Inde Navarrette Teases Her Plan to Nail Rogue’s Southern Accent
highlights.summary: Obsession breakout Inde Navarrette already has a plan to make sure she nails Rogue's iconic Southern accent in the new X-Men movie. Navarrette will jump from horror to the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) when she appears in X-Men in 2028.
body: The character is known for her southern draw, especially thanks to the delivery made popular by original X-Men animated series voice actress Lenore Zann. Navarrette may not have the natural accent audiences would expect from Rogue, but she told Entertainment Tonight that the mutant team member's voice is very much already on her mind.

"I've never told this publicly – I completely forgot – but I have a divorced family. I grew up in Texas for a good majority of my life," Navarrette said when asked how she'll build Rogue's voice. "So, honestly, those Southern women are really my favorite."

Navarrette then noted her specific connection to Corpus Christi, a coastal town located toward the south end of Texas. For the Obsession actress-turned-Marvel superhero, it's the "old Southern women" that she "really, really loves." But her appreciation for the South doesn't stop there.
"But, specifically, Mississippi – Rogue is from Mississippi," she continued. "So, I really just want to go there. I wanna really do her justice."

highlights.title: Breville Eye Q toaster review: a ‘revolutionary device’ that makes perfect toast without me trying
highlights.summary: I toasted just about every kind of bread in Breville’s new Eye Q – and each slice came out perfectly toasted. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things. It’s a centuries-old problem: how to prepare the perfect slice of toast.
body: The core technology of the toaster has changed little in the past 100 years. A coil of high-resistance wires is activated for a certain period, and the radiant heat from that coil warms and browns the bread. The only measure of doneness that a traditional toaster has is time, but, as anyone who has had burnt toast for breakfast knows, time is a very imprecise proxy.

Breville’s new Eye Q toaster aims to change that legacy. Rather than setting a clock to tick until toast pops out, the Eye Q actually “looks” inside the toaster at the bread to determine whether it is done, thanks to a heat-resistant optical sensor that flashes 10 times per second to monitor the browning process. Hence the gadget’s catch phrase: “We watch your toast so you don’t have to.”

“It took us 10 years to get this project right,” Tom Groundes-Peace, global category manager and head of research at Breville, said. Groundes-Peace likens the innovation to the electric car: while cars evolved over the last century, they were all variations powered by an internal combustion engine. Until the electric motor.

highlights.title: Anthropic CEO outlines plan to slow AI development
highlights.summary: Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman seem to agree that it's time to "pace the frontier." What would that actually look like?
body: We’ve been seeing increasingly dire warnings from AI researchers about the dangers of artificial intelligence, and even comments from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman that it may be time to “pace” AI development. But what would that actually look like?

In a new blog post, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei not only echoed the call to “pace the frontier,” but also outlined three broad strategies for doing so. And he said Anthropic is “unilaterally committing” to one of them, with Altman chiming in to say OpenAI will follow suit.

The debate over AI safety and alignment intensified this week after researcher Jacob Coxon wrote that he’s resigning from Anthropic over concerns that the leading AI companies are “gambling with our lives” while the people building the technology “earnestly believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” a claim repeated by others at Anthropic.
points: Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman seem to agree that it's time to "pace the frontier.

highlights.title: OpenAI just wants to win
highlights.summary: OpenAI has spent the last few years planting flags across the increasingly difficult terrain in mathematics. This week, it claimed one of its biggest prizes yet: a solution to a legendary Millennium Prize problem. In normal circumstances, this would have been celebrated as a historic achievement.
body: Two mathematicians at the heart of recent controversies tell The Verge how AI giants’ ‘childish’ rivalries are upending the field.

Instead, many mathematicians have watched OpenAI’s relentless advance with growing unease. To them, the company appears less like an enthusiastic newcomer than an impossibly well-resourced interloper, charging into problems they have dedicated their lives to studying with little apparent regard for long-standing norms or the consequences for those left in its wake. At the heart of that unease is a sense that OpenAI is doing mathematics for different reasons. Mathematicians want to advance the field. OpenAI wants to win.
Mathematics is not normally this dramatic, so how did things get this bad?

This week, The Verge spoke with more than a dozen mathematicians, including Tristan Buckmaster and Andreas Thom, who are at the center of recent controversies surrounding OpenAI’s work in the field. Even those skeptical of the most serious allegations described a field shaken by the tech giant’s conduct and fearful of what it might do next in its determination to trounce its rivals.
points: OpenAI has spent the last few years planting flags across the increasingly difficult terrain in mathematics.
This week, it claimed one of its biggest prizes yet: a solution to a legendary Millennium Prize problem.

highlights.title: Woman Unknown wins Venice film festival as NAZA takes special jury prize
highlights.summary: May el-Toukhy becomes eighth female director to take Golden Lion as Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love and Guardian-produced exposé of Israel’s Gaza killings also awarded. Bold and bravura choices as Venice celebrates A Woman Unknown, Possible Love – and NAZA.
body: May el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown has scooped the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival, at an awards ceremony that also saw the Gaza documentary NAZA win the jury prize.

Set in the immediate aftermath of Danish liberation from Nazi occupation, the Egyptian-Danish director’s film tells the story of a young housemaid, Marie (Mathilde Arcel), who is about to marry her widowed employer but anxious about him discovering a shameful secret in her past: during the war, Marie had an intimate relationship with a German soldier.
The Guardian’s film critic hailed Woman Unknown as “elegantly appointed” in his review, likening it to Alfred Hitchcock’s Rebecca.

Arcel also won the festival’s best actress prize, the Volpi Cup, which puzzled some critics: usually, Venice doesn’t award more than one prize to a film. Speaking to the press after the ceremony, the jury president, Maggie Gyllenhaal, said they were able to make an exception because the jury’s vote for the Danish actor was unanimous. “She is going to blow our socks off,” she said.
points: Bold and bravura choices as Venice celebrates A Woman Unknown, Possible Love – and NAZA.

A checked pattern taken from O’Keeffe’s distinctive capsule wardrobe of utilitarian chic appeared on this catwalk as a wrap coat, hardware-free with a fabric belt and no buttons.

One nod to pop culture was allowed: a model in a crepe-back satin ivory slip dress, her blond hair scraped back by a simple headband, called to mind the late Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy, the iconic Calvin Klein employee who was launched back into the fashion conversation by Ryan Murphy’s Love Story earlier this year.

They looked like pieces from Alexander Calder’s huge mobile, Lobster Trap and Fish Tail, which hangs in the stairwell of the museum.

highlights.summary: Plus: The US disrupts the internet’s biggest black market, a Conti ransomware hacker gets prison time, Meta fails to stop AI-generated videos of child abuse.
body: Editor’s note: After more than a decade, this is the last WIRED Security News This Week. “The roundup,” as we call it internally, started as a way to ensure that our readers knew about the latest key cybersecurity and privacy news even if we didn’t write about it ourselves. It was a simple way to highlight our own work and the wealth of other great journalism and research published in this realm every week.

Over the years, the roundup has developed a devoted following, and some editions have even become viral hits—which is honestly weird, but the cybersecurity community is great and weird, so it feels right. Rest assured that something new and exciting is coming in the roundup’s place, so stay tuned for that! For now, as always, stay safe out there.

Meta failed to catch roughly 350 AI child abuse ads, according to new research this week, including some that included images of real kids. In one case, a child depicted in an ad was a member of a European royal family. Lawmakers have said they intend to investigate, and the San Francisco City Attorney’s Office ordered the company this week to stop “allowing” AI child abuse ads.
